title: Ireland: employment permits and non-EEA family reunification

laws.title: Employment Permits Act 2024 (No. 17 of 2024): who needs a permit, the critical skills employment permit, the 50 percent rule, grounds for refusal and the power to make regulations
laws.amendment: Changed by later Acts of the Oireachtas. The eISB legislation directory for the Act, updated to 2026-10-21, lists its commencement orders (S.I. No. 443 of 2024 and S.I. No. 32 of 2025) and, as the only amendments, insertions into s. 8(1) and a change to s. 8(3) by the International Protection Act 2026, s. 313, not yet commenced. The eISB page is the Act as enacted. Pay thresholds, occupation lists and most other detail sit in regulations made under ss. 4 and 47.

laws.title: Employment Permits Regulations 2024 (S.I. No. 444 of 2024): the principal regulations, with Part 5 on critical skills employment permits, fees in Schedule 1 and Schedules 3 and 4 as first made
laws.amendment: Made by the Minister under the 2024 Act, in operation from 2024-09-02, and amended often by Employment Permits (Amendment) Regulations, which s. 4(4) of the Act requires to be laid before each House: 2 sets in late 2024, 5 in 2025, then S.I. No. 213 and S.I. No. 558 of 2026. The eISB page shows the instrument as made, with no amendment applied, so its pay amounts and Schedules 3 and 4 are out of date; read it with every amending instrument. The pay thresholds are reviewed every year under s. 47(4) of the Act.

laws.title: Employment Permits (Amendment) (No. 5) Regulations 2025 (S.I. No. 643 of 2025): from 2026-03-01, eligible employments, qualifications and the Schedule 8 minimum pay for critical skills permits
laws.amendment: Made on 2025-12-17 by the Minister of State; regulations 18 to 20 came into operation on the day made and the rest on 2026-03-01. Its Schedule 8 holds the minimum remuneration for every permit type; S.I. No. 558 of 2026 has already replaced Part 10, for seasonal permits. Under s. 47(4) of the Act the Minister reviews the amounts every year against CSO average weekly earnings and must raise them by at least the increase found, so look each year for an instrument amending Schedule 8. The 2025 roadmap review marks the January 2027 critical skills figures as to be determined.

laws.title: Employment Permits (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (S.I. No. 213 of 2026), made 2026-05-13: Schedule 3 (critical skills occupations) and Schedule 4 (ineligible employments) replaced
laws.amendment: States no commencement date, so under s. 16(3) of the Interpretation Act 2005 it came into operation at the end of 2026-05-12, the day before it was made; notice of its making appeared in Iris Oifigiúil on 2026-05-22. It also amends Schedule 2 and replaces Schedule 5. Its Schedules 3 and 4 were replaced again by S.I. No. 558 of 2026, made 2026-10-28, so its lists govern only the months between.

laws.title: Employment Permits (Amendment) (No. 2) Regulations 2026 (S.I. No. 558 of 2026), made 2026-10-28: Schedules 3 and 4 replaced again, and changes to seasonal permits, including Part 10 of Schedule 8
laws.amendment: States no commencement date, so under s. 16(3) of the Interpretation Act 2005 it came into operation at the end of 2026-10-27, though notice of its making appeared in Iris Oifigiúil only on 2026-11-06. When read, eISB held it only as a PDF, with no HTML page. Section 47(16) of the Act requires the Minister to review the regulations from time to time, on no fixed date; Schedule 3 has been changed by amending instruments 4 times since 2025 (S.I. Nos. 64 and 643 of 2025, 213 and 558 of 2026).

laws.title: Immigration Act 1999, s. 1(1): a non-national is an alien under the Aliens Act 1935, other than an alien whom an order under s. 10 of that Act exempts from all of it
laws.amendment: The page shows s. 1 as enacted, still naming the Minister for Justice, Equality and Law Reform. The eISB legislation directory for the Act, updated to 2026-10-21, lists no amendment of s. 1. The Employment Permits Act 2024, s. 2(1), defines a foreign national by this definition of non-national, so a change here changes who needs an employment permit.

laws.title: Aliens Act 1935, s. 2: an alien is a person who is not a citizen of Saorstát Eireann
laws.amendment: The page shows s. 2 as enacted in 1935. The eISB legislation directory for the Act, updated to 2026-10-21, lists no change to s. 2 and records art. 3 of the Aliens (Exemption) Order 1999 as restricting the Act’s application. Under s. 10(1) of the Act, as recited in that Order, the Government may by order exempt the citizens of a country from any of its provisions.

laws.title: Aliens (Exemption) Order 1999 (S.I. No. 97 of 1999), art. 3: every citizen of the United Kingdom is exempted from the Aliens Act 1935 and from the aliens orders made under its s. 5
laws.amendment: Made by the Government on 1999-04-20 under s. 10(1) of the Aliens Act 1935. The eISB page shows the order as made, with an Amendments link that lists later changes.

laws.title: European Communities (Amendment) Act 1993, ss. 3 and 4: the EEA Agreement given the force of law, and references to Member States read as including the other EEA states where needed
laws.amendment: Inserted s. 2(2) into the European Communities Act 1972. The European Communities Acts are construed together as one Act and are extended by later amending Acts, such as the 2001 Swiss Act and the 2012 Act. The eISB page is the 1993 Act as enacted.

laws.title: European Communities and Swiss Confederation Act 2001: the 1999 agreement between the European Community and its Member States and Switzerland on the free movement of persons given the force of law
laws.amendment: Inserted s. 2(3) into the European Communities Act 1972 and is construed with the European Communities Acts as one Act. The Department's page on who needs an employment permit says it came into operation on 2002-06-01. The eISB page is the Act as enacted.

laws.title: European Communities (Amendment) Act 2012, s. 1: the definition of the treaties governing the European Union in the European Communities Act 1972, which s. 8(1)(e) of the 2024 Act relies on
laws.amendment: Substituted the definition inserted by the European Union Act 2009, adding among others the 2011 accession treaty of Croatia; s. 8(1)(e) of the 2024 Act cites the European Communities Acts 1972 to 2012. The eISB page is the 2012 Act as enacted.

laws.title: Interpretation Act 2005, s. 16: when an Act or a statutory instrument comes into operation
laws.amendment: The general statute on reading Acts and statutory instruments; the page shows s. 16 as enacted. It decides the start of any amending instrument that states no date, or names a day.

laws.title: Interpretation Act 2005, s. 18(d): a child includes an adopted child and, in an Act passed on or after 1988-01-14, a child adopted outside the State whose adoption is recognised in the State
laws.amendment: The page shows s. 18 as enacted. The Family Reunification Policy borrows its definition of an adopted child, so a change to s. 18(d) changes which adopted children the policy counts.

laws.title: Age of Majority Act 1985, s. 4: a person attains an age at the start of the relevant anniversary of the date of birth
laws.amendment: The page shows s. 4 as enacted. Subsection (3) ties the date of turning 18 to the electoral calculation, but only for the electoral, presidential, Seanad, referendum, local and European election Acts it lists.

laws.title: Policy Document on Non-EEA Family Reunification, Immigration Service Delivery, Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, 2026-06-12: who may join a critical skills permit holder
laws.amendment: A scheme under the Minister's discretionary executive power (para. 1.1), not a statute. ISD revises it by publishing a new version of the document, as it did from 2026-06-12. Its Appendix D figures are to be updated annually (footnote 44), and ISD's notice says other thresholds rise in line with indexation.

laws.title: Immigration Service Delivery notice: amendments to the non-EEA Family Reunification Policy take effect from 2026-06-12
laws.amendment: A news notice dated 2026-06-12 that summarises the changes and links the revised policy; the policy document itself is the text to read.

laws.title: Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Critical Skills Employment Permit page: criteria, remuneration, fee, family reunification and Stamp 4
laws.amendment: Departmental guidance, not law, with no date on the page. It shows the thresholds in force from 2026-03-01 but still names former bodies such as the Department of Justice and Equality and the Irish Naturalisation and Immigration Service, and it differs from the regulations in places; the regulations are the law.

laws.title: Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Who needs an employment permit: non-EEA nationals need one; Swiss nationals and holders of some permissions do not
laws.amendment: Departmental guidance, not law, signed Economic Migration Policy Unit 2021 though it cites the Employment Permits Act 2024.

laws.title: Employment Permits Minimum Annual Remuneration: Outcome of the Roadmap Review 2025, Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
laws.amendment: A policy review, not law: its 2026 thresholds took effect only through S.I. No. 643 of 2025, from 2026-03-01. Its table lists the January 2027 critical skills thresholds with and without a relevant degree as to be determined, and the critical skills graduate rate as index only.

pitfalls.text: The eISB text of S.I. No. 444 of 2024 shows the regulations as made: regulations 25 and 26 still print EUR 38,000 (EUR 18.74 an hour) for Schedule 3 jobs and EUR 64,000 (EUR 31.56) for other jobs. From 2026-03-01, S.I. No. 643 of 2025 substituted regulation 25 and paragraphs (a) and (b) of regulation 26 and inserted Schedule 8, whose Part 1 sets EUR 40,904 (EUR 20.17), EUR 36,848 (EUR 18.17) and EUR 68,911 (EUR 33.98). The made text of the principal regulations is no authority for a current amount.

Section 47(4) of the Act requires the Minister, every year from the making of the regulations concerned, to review each minimum remuneration against the latest CSO average weekly earnings and, where they rose, to raise it by at least that percentage. The Department’s 2025 roadmap review marks the January 2027 critical skills figures as to be determined and the graduate rate as index only. The 2026-03-01 amounts apply until a new amending instrument takes effect, and no text read states the next figures.

Section 32(7) of the Act, subject to ss. 44(5) and 45(5), requires refusal where a grant would contravene the s. 47 regulations in force when the decision is made, and S.I. No. 643 of 2025 has no transitional provision for applications made before 2026-03-01. The Department’s roadmap review says instead that a threshold applies at the point of application, and that the January 2024 increases affected applications received from that date. The texts point different ways, and none settles which amounts govern an application pending across a change.

Since 2026-03-01 regulation 25 makes every employment eligible except those in Schedule 4. A Schedule 3 job needs EUR 40,904 and a relevant third level degree, or for a nurse, midwife or radiographer a degree or diploma their registration board accepts (reg. 27(1)); EUR 36,848 applies only to a reg. 27(1)(c) degree at level 8 or higher, or equivalent, obtained in the 12 months before the application. Any other eligible job needs EUR 68,911 and a relevant degree or the necessary experience (reg. 27(2)). The Department’s page gives the lower rate for any qualification in those 12 months.

For a Schedule 3 job bound by a public sector pay agreement, including in bodies funded under s. 38 of the Health Act 2004, or by a Workplace Relations Commission pay agreement linked to one for community and voluntary organisation employments, regulation 26(b) sets the minimum as the pay in that agreement, not Schedule 8.

Remuneration under s. 3(1)(a) of the Act is the salary, at an hourly rate not below the national minimum or a higher rate fixed by an enactment, plus any health insurance payment; board and accommodation count only for 3 other permit types (s. 3(1)(b) and (c)). It is the remuneration proposed in the application (s. 3(2)(a)), excluding bonuses per the Department’s page. The annual minimum is the pay for 39 hours a week for 52 weeks (s. 47(3)) and is not reduced for fewer minimum hours (s. 48(2)(a)); that a 20-hour job, the reg. 29 minimum, still needs the full figure is an inference.

Section 22(1) bars a permit unless, on the date of application, at least half the employer’s employees are EEA nationals, Swiss nationals or citizens of the United Kingdom, in any combination; s. 2(2) counts the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man as part of the United Kingdom. The Department’s page mentions only EEA nationals.

For a critical skills permit, s. 22(2) lifts the 50 percent rule only where all 3 hold: the employer has been registered with the Revenue Commissioners for the prescribed period on the day of application, Enterprise Ireland or IDA Ireland has recommended the application, and the Minister is satisfied the grant will contribute to developing employment. Regulation 13 prescribes registration for 2 years on the day the application is made, while the Department’s page describes start-ups within 2 years of registering as an employer. The wordings differ.

Section 7 of the Act binds only a foreign national: by s. 2(1) a non-national under the Immigration Act 1999, that is an alien under the Aliens Act 1935 other than one to whom, by an order under its s. 10, none of that Act applies. Article 3 of the Aliens (Exemption) Order 1999 exempts every citizen of the United Kingdom from the provisions of the 1935 Act. No text read says in one place whether a British citizen is a foreign national needing a permit; the Department’s page omits them, and the Order does not define a UK citizen.

Section 8(1)(e) disapplies s. 7 for a foreign national entitled to enter and work in the State under the treaties governing the European Union, which the 1972 Act, as amended in 2012, defines as the EU treaties and the Community treaties. The 1993 and 2001 Acts give the EEA Agreement and the EU-Swiss free movement agreement the force of law and, so far as needed, read references to Member States as including those states. No text read says in one place that s. 8(1)(e) reaches EEA and Swiss nationals; the Department’s page says non-EEA nationals need a permit and Swiss nationals do not.

S.I. No. 213 and S.I. No. 558 of 2026, made on 2026-05-13 and 2026-10-28, state no commencement date, so under s. 16(3) of the Interpretation Act 2005 each came into operation at the end of the day before it was made; the later notices in Iris Oifigiúil are not the start. S.I. No. 643 of 2025 names 2026-03-01, so under s. 16(4) it came into operation at the end of 2026-02-28. When read, eISB held S.I. No. 558 only as a PDF, and the 2024 Act’s directory, updated to 2026-10-21, did not list it, so the year’s list of statutory instruments and the PDFs can be newer than the HTML pages.

Schedule 3 lists jobs by SOC 2010 codes at 3 and 4 digit level, and some entries carry their own conditions: an academic needs a qualification equivalent to level 10 of the National Framework of Qualifications awarded at least 2 calendar years before the application, at least one academic year of relevant teaching, and a qualifying institution or programme; several 2D or 3D animation roles need at least a year in the role. The entry, not a job title, decides. ICT professionals in SOC 2133 to 2139 are listed in both 2026 versions of the Schedule.

Family rules come from the Family Reunification Policy, a discretionary executive scheme with no automatic entitlement (paras. 1.1 and 1.2), not the 2024 Act. A permit holder is a Category B sponsor: the nuclear family may accompany on arrival with no waiting period once all requirements are met and any entry visas obtained (para. 6.3), even before any earnings accrue (para. 10.8), and gets Stamp 1G (Appendix C). The EUR 30,000 couple threshold and the minor children figures, such as a net EUR 39,780 for one child in 2026, bind Category C sponsors (paras. 10.11 and 10.13), not Category B.

A spouse, civil partner or de facto partner must be at least 18 at the time of their own application (paras. 7.5 and 7.12). For a child the policy names no date, saying only that unmarried children under 18 are nuclear family (para. 7.22), and processing takes about 12 months (para. 1.12). Section 4(1) of the Age of Majority Act 1985 says an age is attained at the start of the relevant anniversary of the date of birth; it says nothing about a 29 February birthday.

A de facto partnership is a relationship akin to marriage, duly attested, including at least 2 years of cohabitation before the application (glossary; para. 7.13 makes it an important factor). The partner must not be related to the sponsor by family and the relationship must be exclusive for the whole qualifying period (para. 7.12). The 2 years are of cohabitation, not only of the relationship. Where a party is still married to someone else, the case is discretionary and a qualifying period generally runs from the legal separation (para. 7.15).

A marriage or civil partnership must be between 2 people only, freely entered into, lawfully conducted and capable of recognition under Irish law (para. 7.6); a civil partnership made in Ireland before 2016-05-16, or abroad where civil partnerships are recognised, counts as marriage (para. 7.10). Only the first marriage is recognised: a later one made while it subsists never counts, even after a divorce, and a second or later spouse is refused (para. 7.17). Evidence should show the parties met in person before and since the marriage (para. 7.8), and for a proxy marriage must (para. 7.20).

A child is the sponsor’s biological child, step-child, or adopted child within s. 18 of the Interpretation Act 2005 (para. 7.21); the adoption must have been made in Ireland or be recognised under Irish law (para. 7.24.1). Only unmarried children under 18 are nuclear family (para. 7.22). Stepchildren are treated as immediate family when shown to be full-time members of the household (para. 7.26); the policy neither defines a step-child nor says whether a de facto partner’s child is one. If parents are divorced, separated or estranged, the other parent must consent (Appendix B).

A Category B sponsor can apply for dependent parents and adult children only after 2 years in the State on an eligible permission immediately before applying (para. 6.3), and must have earned in Ireland gross income above 185 percent of average yearly earnings for 1 relative, or 250 percent for 2, in each of the previous 3 years (para. 10.19; EUR 96,929 and EUR 130,985 in 2026, Appendix D). The relatives must first apply for Stamp 0 from outside the State (para. 10.17), and an adult child must depend on the sponsor’s care through a serious medical or psychological condition (para. 7.23).

Visa-required family members must apply before travelling, and others must tell the immigration officer at entry that they will apply; no application is accepted for a family member already in the State on another permission, with none, or as a visitor (paras. 3.5.1 and 3.5.2). Sponsors in all categories must not live in homeless, emergency, IPAS, social or local authority housing (para. 9.4), a change ISD’s notice records from 2026-06-12. The family’s residence depends on the sponsor’s continued residence and status (para. 16.1).

The Minister must refuse where someone was dismissed by reason of redundancy from the same employment in the 6 months before the application, or the employer is not registered with the Revenue Commissioners or, if carrying on a business, has no substantive business operations in the State (s. 32(1) and (2)). The offer must be made in the 90 days before the application, 120 for an academic or third level institution (reg. 10), the job must start within 6 months of the grant or stated start (reg. 17), and a holder on a first permit is expected to stay 9 months with the first employer (reg. 18).
